Environmental Ed Day 14 Visiting Megamuch

Oct 29, 2010 • Janice Cotcher

The Royal Sask Museum is one of my favorite places in Regina and I try to visit it a couple times a year. The first time I visited the RSM was for a a field trip in kindergarten. Back then all the displays were behind glass and my class were very strictly instructed not to touch. Who were they kidding? Of course a large group of 5 year olds are going to touch the glass. We’d race from exhibit to exhibit to be the first one arrive to get the best spot for viewing. The only time I arrived first was at the bison exhibit. Just as luck would have it, the glass was out being replaced and I ran and fell face first into the exhibit. I’m probably one of the few people who remembers what the RSM was like before the fire in 1990. It is really a shame that they were unable to replace the bison exhibit but certainly understandable.

I’ve always been fascinated with bison since my maternal grandparents live near Canada’s only free-ranging herd within its historic range. Some family members were integral in founding the Sturgeon River Plains Bison Stewards, an organization working so the bison can co-exist with local ranchers in a mutually beneficial way. I have suggested to the other science majors that we visit the Prince Albert National Park to see the Sturgeon River Plains bison herd and speak with the stewards for class trip.

Of course, my favorite addition to the museum is Megamunch! ! My friend Alicia has been to the museum many times but never knew Megamunch existed. I insisted we get a picture with him.

The main reason for our visit was to see the Human Factor exhibit. I’ve seen the exhibit many times before but got a lot more out of it after our visit from the curator. For example, I never knew that some of the sculptures where called the “Towers of Power”: ! Humans are standing on a pile of garbage denoting what we have conquered can come crashing down at anytime. That’s deep.

I didn’t have time to take the Ecological Footprint challenge while I was at the museum but I took it online when I got home. I got 3.8 hectares this time and I think over a year ago I got about 4.6 hectares. That is an improvement but it really should be below 2 hectares per person with the current world population. I have been procrastinating to get a vermicast started for my family but I think the time is now. I certainly need to think of other ways to reduce my footprint.
